We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments regarding the origin of performance improvements in nonlinear networks. To address whether these gains stem from increased network depth or intrinsic nonlinear properties, we perform comprehensive analyses and additional controlled experiments.
A key feature of our architecture is that each nonlinear layer employs globally shared parameters, specifically, all 14×14 units within a nonlinear layer utilize identical threshold and slope values. Thus, adding a nonlinear layer introduces only two trainable parameters (threshold and slope), making its contribution to the total parameter count negligible.
To rigorously decouple the effects of depth from nonlinearity, we design a matched six-layer linear control network with identical parameterization. Specifically, we compared 3 networks:
1) A baseline three-layer linear network (22×22 independently tunable units per layer, 1,452 total parameters);
2) A network comprising three linear layers interleaved with three nonlinear layers, with the nonlinear layers contributing only six extra parameters (total parameters: 1,458);
3) A novel six-layer linear network where the additional three layers apply globally consistent linear modulation (two parameters per layer, aptitude and phase, six in total), maintaining both the total parameter count (1,458) and network depth identical to the nonlinear net.

Comment 2.4:
In the dataset-based recognition tasks for both MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, as outlined in Supplementary Note 4, you describe a process in which the original 28×28-pixel grayscale images are first down sampled to 14×14 pixels using interpolation. Following this, a binarization is applied, where pixel values exceeding a threshold of 0.15 are set to 1. While this down sampling and binarization process is a standard approach in some image processing tasks, it is important to note that the binarization step can have a significant impact on dataset difficulty and model performance. By reducing pixel precision, one inevitably loses valuable information, which could directly contribute to a decrease in recognition accuracy. It would be beneficial to discuss the potential effects of this binarization on the presented results, as understanding its impact is crucial for readers evaluating the robustness of this approach.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewers’ valuable comments. We fully agree that the binarization of input images would impact model performance. To systematically evaluate the effects of down sampling and binarization on recognition performance, we conducted comparative experiments on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets. These experiments employed three types of input: original images, down sampled images, and down sampled and binarized images, tested separately in purely linear and nonlinear networks.
The results reveal distinct performance trends. For Fashion-MNIST, the linear network achieves accuracies of 78.00% (original images), 76.98% (down sampled images), and 74.43% (down sampled + binarized images) for the three input types, as shown in Fig. R21. While the nonlinear network attains 83.71%, 82.68%, and 78.80% respectively Fig.R22. Similarly, on MNIST, the linear network achieves 91.28%, 91.07%, and 88.63% (Fig.R23), whereas the nonlinear network reaches 94.78%, 94.68%, and 92.81% (Fig.R24). These findings demonstrate that while down sampling has a relatively minor effect on accuracy, binarization leads to a more substantial performance decline of 2–5%, consistent with the reviewers’ observation that binarization discards valuable image information.
We adopt binarization primarily for two reasons. First, our study focuses on comparing the relative performance of nonlinear versus linear networks under identical input conditions, making input consistency more critical than absolute accuracy. Second, binarization significantly reduces control circuit complexity, a key consideration for our hardware implementation.
We acknowledge the limitations of this down sampling and binarization process and explicitly discuss the performance trade-offs in the revised manuscript. To address these limitations, we propose future enhancements, including the integration of a DAC module to enable approximately continuous grayscale input processing. This modification, compatible with our current input layer architecture, is expected to preserve richer image details and improve recognition accuracy while retaining circuit simplicity. This refinement will better balance performance and implementation complexity. More details and analyses are available in our response to Comment 1.4.

The binarization process inevitably leads to a decrease in performance, even when employing fully digital neural networks. In other words, can the observed decrease in accuracy be more a result of the dataset transformation, rather than a limitation of the MN-DNN model itself? Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewers’ valuable comments. Regarding your concern about the impact of binarization on model performance, we conduct an in-depth comparative study. Through comprehensive simulation and comparative analysis, we confirm that the reduction in classification accuracy on the Fashion-MNIST dataset is predominantly attributable to the dataset transformation (the downsampling and binarization operations) rather than any fundamental constraints of the MN-DNN model.
We would analyze the MN-DNN’s accuracy from two key aspects:
(1) Performance comparison on traditional digital neural networks
(2) Performance comparison on other nonlinear DNNs
Performance comparison on traditional digital neural networks
To systematically evaluate the respective effects of dataset preprocessing and model architecture, we carefully design a fully connected network (FCN) with comparable parameters to MN-DNN, as well as a more representative CNN model as benchmarks. Specifically, the FCN adopts a three-layer structure of 196-7-10, totaling 1,459 parameters, which is highly comparable to MN-DNN’s 1,458 parameters. Additionally, we construct a CNN architecture (approximately 106,000 parameters) comprising convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers to investigate the effects of deeper feature extraction. Both models use the same 14×14 binarized input images as MN-DNN.
The experimental results demonstrate that on the binarized MNIST dataset, the FCN, CNN, and MN-DNN achieve accuracies of 85.97% (FCN, Fig. R25), 93.57% (CNN, Fig.R26), and 92.83% (MN-DNN), respectively. On the more challenging Fashion-MNIST dataset, the accuracies are 75.46% (FCN, Fig.R27), 83.22% (CNN, Fig.R28), and 78.8%(MN-DNN), respectively (see Table R11 for the comparative results). MN-DNN performs comparably to or even better than the nonlinear FCN, while being lower but still competitive with the CNN.
Remarkably, MN-DNN achieves classification performance close to that of traditional digital neural networks, which strongly validates the effectiveness of its architecture. We agree that the performance decline primarily stems from information loss due to the binarization process, rather than inherent limitations in MN-DNN’s design.

Comment 2.8:
The manuscript does not provide a detailed discussion of the number of trainable parameters, which is a crucial aspect for understanding the model's complexity and scalability. It would be beneficial for the authors to explicitly mention the total number of trainable parameters and offer a comparison with those typically found in conventional neural networks. Furthermore, the number of trainable parameters associated with both the linear and non-linear layers should be clearly specified to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the model's architecture and its computational demands. A more thorough discussion in this regard would improve the transparency of the model's design and facilitate a clearer comparison with existing approaches in the literature.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer’s valuable feedback. In response to the comments regarding the trainable parameters in our model, we have conducted a comprehensive review and analysis. Below, we provide a detailed clarification:
Model Architecture and Parameter Efficiency
The linear component of our model comprises three linear layers, each containing 22×22 = 484 trainable phase parameters constrained within the range [0, 2π]. This results in a total of 1,452 trainable parameters for the linear network, as shown in Fig.R29. In contrast, the nonlinear network extends this structure by introducing three nonlinear layers. Each nonlinear layer consists of 14×14 computational units that operate under a shared state, meaning all units within a layer utilize the same nonlinear threshold and slope. Consequently, each nonlinear layer requires training only two key parameters, the threshold and slope of the ReLU activation function. This design enables the nonlinear network to achieve complex transformations while introducing only six additional parameters, yielding a total of 1,458 trainable parameters, as shown in Fig.R30.

Comparative Efficiency with Traditional Neural Networks
Our model demonstrates remarkable parameter efficiency compared to conventional deep learning architectures. For instance, standard fully connected networks for MNIST classification typically require tens to hundreds of thousands of parameters, while even lightweight CNNs such as LeNet-5 demand approximately 60,000 parameters. In contrast, our architecture achieves competitive performance with only ~1,500 parameters—an order of magnitude reduction in model size. This extreme parameter efficiency positions our model within the TinyML (Tiny Machine Learning), domain, yet it retains high recognition accuracy while significantly improving computational efficiency.
Scalability and Flexibility
Notably, our architecture exhibits exceptional scalability. By adjusting the network dimensions (e.g., expanding each linear layer to 56×56 units), the total trainable parameters can be increased by ~9,414, reaching a scale (~10,000 parameters) comparable to conventional fully connected networks. This flexibility allows the model to maintain its lightweight advantages while adapting to more demanding computational tasks without substantial increases in inference time. Such scalability ensures broad applicability across varying complexity requirements while preserving efficiency.

Supplementary Figure S22 | Output plane power detection device. a, Photograph of the MN-DNN system’s output plane detection device. b, Back view of the output plane detection device. c, Photograph of an individual RF power detection circuit board. d, Photograph of an individual detection circuit board connected to the MCU and LED.
For fast output detection, we replace the conventional two-dimensional near-field scanning platform with a rapid output plane detection device, which measures ten regions on the output plane, as shown in Supplementary Figure 22a. The output plane is positioned 10 cm away from the last layer of the hidden layer. A large acrylic plate is supported at the output plane, with 10 designated areas each equipped with a patch antenna and detector to detect the power distribution across the output plane. Additionally, an MCU and an LED (not shown in the figure, located on the side) are mounted on the setup to provide real-time comparison of the energy in the 10 areas and to display the classification results.
Supplementary Figure S22b depicts a back view of the output plane detection apparatus. 10 patch antennas are secured to an acrylic board using plastic screws, positioned at 10 distinct regions designated for output energy detection. The central frequency of these patch antennas matches the operational frequency of the MN-DNN, which is 5.8GHz. Each patch antenna is interfaced with a circuit board designed to perform RF amplification and RF detection, which transforms the RF energy captured by the patch antenna into an equivalent direct current (DC) voltage. The detection circuits are mounted on L-shaped acrylic panels using plastic screws, which are then affixed to the larger acrylic panel via the same fastening technique. The electrical connections for each detection circuit are configured in parallel to maintain a uniform DC voltage bias across all circuits, thus standardizing the performance characteristics of each detection circuit. Supplementary Figure S22c presents a photographic representation of a detection circuit that incorporates a two-stage amplifier and a detector component.
Supplementary Figure S22d provides a photographic illustration of the interface between the detection circuit, the microcontroller unit (MCU) Arduino DUE R3, and the light-emitting diode (LED). The output voltage from the detection circuit is connected to the MCU's analog-to-digital converter (ADC) input for digitization. This digital signal is then subjected to a comparison process across 10 discrete ports. Based on the port exhibiting the highest voltage reading, the MCU generates a corresponding code to regulate the color of the LED. Additionally, the classification result associated with the port exhibiting the highest voltage value is returned to the computer in real-time through serial communication with the MCU Arduino DUE R3. 
Supplementary Figure S23 illustrates the complete equivalent circuit of the high-speed detection system. The device operates as follows: A host computer communicates with an STM32 MCU via a serial interface, which orchestrates the encoding of the input plane. By precisely modulating the voltage applied to each unit cell in the input layer, the input image is spatially encoded onto the transmission coefficients of the metasurface. EM waves then propagate through the encoded input plane, traversing the diffractive neural network before reaching the output plane. At the output plane, RF signals detected by an array of 10 patch antennas undergo amplification via a two-stage RF amplifier. Each amplification stage provides tunable gain (0–10 dB) through voltage-controlled (V ) regulation, yielding a total adjustable gain of 0–20 dB. This wide dynamic range ensures CTRL robust detection of RF signals across varying intensities. The amplified signals are synchronously sampled and digitized through the MCU’s ADC channels. Classification is determined by identifying the channel with the highest output voltage, with results visually indicated via an LED display and simultaneously logged on the host computer for further analysis. Using this optimized detection system, we demonstrate efficient classification of 5,000 test images using both linear and nonlinear diffractive network configurations, with the nonlinear network achieving superior performance (92.4% accuracy) compared to its linear counterpart (88.5%).

Remarks to the Author:
The paper by Ning et al presents a highly novel contribution to the field of diffractive neural networks (DNNs) by introducing a multilayer nonlinear diffractive neural network (MN-DNN) operating in the microwave band. This system leverages programmable metasurfaces integrated with RF amplifiers, detectors, and voltage adders to implement a tunable ReLU-like nonlinear activation function with an impressive 4.5 ns latency, significantly faster than the millisecond/microsecond latencies of conventional optoelectronic methods. The MN-DNN's ability to adjust activation thresholds and slopes via bias voltages enables real-time reconfiguration, addressing the rigidity of prior optical DNNs. Additionally, its low-power nonlinear processing and direct electromagnetic (EM) wave processing for tasks like human posture classification set it apart from existing approaches, which often rely on high-energy inputs or digital encoding. The research represents an impactful contribution to both research and practical deployment. I am happy to recommend its publication in Nature Communications provided the authors could address the following points.

Comment 4.2:
There seems to be no mention of the operating frequency of the metasurface DNN. Would it be possible to increase the operating frequency so that the system can be more compact?
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comments. First, we would like to apologize for the insufficient clarity regarding the operating frequency in the original manuscript. In fact, the working frequency of the MN-DNN is 5.8 GHz. Following the reviewer's suggestion, we have supplemented detailed explanations of the relevant frequency parameters in the revised manuscript.
Regarding to the reviewer’s suggestion to enhance system compactness by increasing the operating frequency, we fully agree with this perspective. From a technical implementation standpoint, elevating the system's operating frequency can indeed effectively reduce device dimensions, thereby achieving overall system miniaturization. Specifically, this optimization can be advanced synergistically from two dimensions: active devices and passive structures. For active devices, adopting higher-frequency RF components (such as millimeter-wave/terahertz low-noise amplifiers based on InP HEMT [R38], SiGe [R39-R40], or CMOS [R38] processes, as well as high-frequency detectors [R42-R43] like the PE80T3002 or VDI ZBD) can readily extend the system's operating frequency to the millimeter-wave or even terahertz range. For passive structures, through reasonable scaling design, the existing antenna and metasurface unit structures can be fully adapted to higher operating frequency bands. This holistic optimization approach not only maintains system performance but also significantly enhances integration density.
Based on the reviewers' suggestions, we will prioritize increasing the operating frequency as a key direction for future research, focusing on exploring the feasibility of achieving high-performance compact nonlinear DNN systems in the millimeter-wave and even terahertz frequency bands. We once again express our gratitude for the reviewers' constructive feedback.

Comment 4.3:
The authors should discuss the key factors that set the lower limit of latency, and how it can be further reduced.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for their insightful discussion and constructive feedback on this key technical challenge.
Lower limit of latency
The fundamental lower bound of system latency is governed by two principal factors: the hardware response characteristics of the nonlinear layer and the EM wave propagation delay in air.
(1) Hardware-induced latency arises from the cumulative delays in the RF amplifier, RF detector, and voltage adder in the nonlinear layer. These are intrinsically constrained by semiconductor physics and parasitic effects in circuit packaging, representing a fundamental physical limitation. However, such delays can be partially reduced through advancements in device fabrication and soldering techniques.
(2) Propagation delay is dictated by the time of flight of EM waves between the input and output layers, with its value depending on the distance between the input and output layers. The delay can be mitigated through design optimizations, such as higher operational frequencies or refined interlayer architectures.
The interplay of these two factors determines the theoretical minimum latency achievable in the system.
Strategies for further latency reduction
To address the challenge of further reducing system latency, we propose a comprehensive optimization framework encompassing device-level enhancements, nonlinear unit structural refinements, and system-level architectural improvements.
(1) Device-Level Optimization
The adoption of high-performance components is critical for minimizing latency at the nonlinear unit level. By integrating ultra-fast operational amplifiers with slew rates exceeding 500 V/μs (response time <200 ps) and planar-deposited n-type silicon Schottky barrier diode detectors (response time <220 ps), alongside replacing conventional RF amplifiers with low-latency RF diode switches, we would achieve a single nonlinear unit delay below 426 ps (Table R18). This approaches the theoretical lower bound for response times in current nonlinear layer implementations.

(2) Nonlinear Unit Structural Optimization
Relaxing the reconfigurability constraints of activation functions enables significant simplification of nonlinear layer. By eliminating operational amplifiers and retaining only essential nonlinear components, such as detectors and Schottky diodes (Fig. R38), we could further reduce single-layer latency to ~226 ps. This streamlined architecture maintains functionality while substantially improving temporal performance.
Figure R38. Simplified Architecture of Nonlinear Unit.
(3) System-Level Optimization
Moreover, in the design of the system architecture, propagation delay can be decreased by reducing the distance between the input and output layers of the nonlinear diffractive neural network. This reduction is attainable through strategies such as elevating the operational frequency and refining the interlayer configuration, including decreasing layer spacing and streamlining the number of layers, which collectively shorten the signal transmission path.
Overall, the proposed multi-scale optimization strategy, including spanning device selection, nonlinear unit structural refinement, and architectural redesign, provides a systematic approach to achieving sub-nanosecond system latency.

[Discussion]
The system latency can be further reduced through multiple optimization approaches (see Supplementary Note 28 for details). By employing high-performance active components in the nonlinear layer, the time delay can be optimized from the nanosecond down to the picosecond range. For example, using operational amplifiers with high slew rates reduces computational delay to below 200 ps, while fast-response diodes (e.g., rapid Schottky barrier diode detectors) as RF detectors shorten the delay to within 220 ps. Further improvements can be achieved by replacing conventional RF amplifiers with high-speed RF Schottky diode switches (~6 ps), enabling superior response speeds. Theoretical calculations indicate that the single-layer delay can be confined to within 426 ps, comparable to the fastest reported nonlinear layers. With a moderate trade-off in reconfigurability, this delay can be further reduced to 226 ps. Additionally, propagation delay can be effectively minimized by optimizing the nonlinear network architecture, for instance, through increased operational frequency and reduced interlayer spacing, thereby compressing the radial distance between input and output planes.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I would like to thank the authors for responding to my comments. However, there are some points that remain to be clarified:
1- There are different values for latency which I found confusing:
-) 4.5 ns nonlinearity latency in the original manuscript. As I understand, that does not reflect the nonlinearity latency and was mentioned by mistake. The actual nonlinearity latency was 2.3 us. Is that correct? If so, total latency (with low speed electronics) would have been 3*2.3 + 2.407 = 9.307us. Please clarify.
-) 2.48 μs system latency and 17.7 ns nonlinearity latency in the revised manuscript. These seem to be based on new measurements on a complete set of new RF components (high-speed). Basically, a new version of the system has been resubmitted but full system classification measurements have not been repeated. Is that correct?
2- Related to the pervious point: On page 13 of the rebuttal, the authors mention: “This functional equivalence ensures our previously demonstrated performance enhancements (in image classification and in action recognition) remain valid, while achieving a faster response speed”. While generally this can be true, to avoid confusion I have the following comment:
As I understand, full system performance measurements have not been repeated with the high-speed version of the system and test boards are fabricated to show faster nonlinearity separately. Is that the case? If so, which is very useful addition to the paper, this should be clarified. The original lower speed components are removed from the revised supplementary document. If full system performance measurements (i.e. classification experiments) have not been redone, the authors should provide the list of both sets of components and their corresponding results. The total system latency and power consumption for both original and new RF components should be provided. This way the reader will fully understand the system capabilities and what has been actually demonstrated.
To summarize, I think it is OK if the authors have not repeated the classification measurement with the high-speed components as long as the they clearly mention that and include all the relevant information for low and high speed results.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have clearly implemented detailed modifications, and I appreciate the effort they put into the manuscript. A number of minor questions and points of clarification remain regarding methodological details and aspects of the experimental validation to fully demonstrate the robustness and generalizability of the proposed approach. I therefore encourage the authors to provide additional explanations and supporting evidence, which would significantly strengthen the clarity, rigor, and overall impact of the manuscript. In essence I believe the work is appropriate for Nature Communications, given the several following modifications are implemented. Below are my detailed comments, together with responses to the changes authors made earlier.
1- I find the authors’ addition of the Fashion-MNIST classification accuracy directly in the introduction to be appropriate and satisfactory. By explicitly reporting the result alongside the MNIST accuracy, the introduction now provides a clearer and more balanced overview of the model’s performance across both benchmark datasets. In this respect, the authors’ modification sufficiently resolves the concern raised, and the manuscript is improved accordingly. This addition is acceptable.
2- By including examples where both linear and nonlinear networks correctly classify inputs, Figs. 3 and 4 now provide a balanced and accurate representation of performance. This clarifies that the linear network can achieve correct classifications, consistent with its reported accuracies, while the nonlinear network still demonstrates superior class separability. The added explanations and supplementary data further enhance transparency and the completeness of the results.
3- I thank the authors for their detailed response and examples, which are informative. I noted that in the “Action Taken” section, only the accuracies are reported. It should be explicitly stated that the improved performance is not due to increased trainable parameters—the nonlinear layers contribute only a negligible number of parameters. The comparison with linear networks of matched parameter counts confirms that the gains stem mainly from the nonlinearity itself. Including this clarification would make the analysis more complete.
4- The authors’ additional experiments and clarifications regarding the effects of down sampling and binarization on classification accuracy are comprehensive and sufficiently address the concern initially raised. The comparative analyses across MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets demonstrate the trade-offs involved and highlight that while down sampling has relatively minor consequences, binarization introduces a more notable degradation in recognition performance. The explicit inclusion of these results in the revised supplementary materials, along with the discussion of future directions involving DAC-based continuous grayscale inputs, represents a valuable enhancement to the manuscript. In this regard, the results are acceptable, and the corrections made to the article are appropriate.
On the other hand, several important points remain. First, if multi-bit recognition is to be performed in future implementations, the proposed system should be analyzed in greater detail, particularly with respect to its processing speed. It would be highly informative if the authors could provide an explicit analysis on the expected operational speed of the system with a DAC. Specifically, what is the processing speed of each layer in terms of bits per second?
The performance figures reported in the manuscript prompt a methodological question regarding network initialization. Typically, with randomly initialized cascaded layers, one would expect initial accuracies that are inversely proportional to the number of layers, as the network is essentially randomly guessing. (e.g., ~10% for MNIST and Fashion). However, the authors report initial accuracies of 84–85% on MNIST and 70–75% on Fashion-MNIST, which are surprisingly high. Could the authors clarify how the layers are initialized, or if this has any positive influence on the relatively high initial accuracies? If a particular weight initialization strategy is employed, it should be explicitly described in the manuscript, as it may significantly affect reproducibility and understanding of the reported performance.
5- By systematically benchmarking their MN-DNN architecture against fully connected networks (FCN) and convolutional neural networks (CNN) of comparable scale, the authors convincingly demonstrate that the performance reduction on Fashion-MNIST. The comparative results show that MN-DNN performs on par with or better than parameter-matched nonlinear FCNs, while maintaining competitive accuracy with CNNs. The results presented are satisfactory, and the inclusion of the detailed comparative analysis in the supplementary material is appropriate and appreciated.
6- While the reported total system delay of 2.48 μs (corresponding to a refresh rate of 403 kHz) demonstrates fast operation, it is important to clarify the concept of real-time performance. Real-time processing is not solely determined by achieving or exceeding a particular frequency threshold (e.g., 30 Hz). Instead, it is defined by the system’s ability to respond to inputs within a bounded and application-specific time window. The latency must consistently satisfy the timing constraints dictated by the intended use case. Although the presented latency values indicate that the system operates well within typical real-time bounds, a discussion explicitly linking these delays to the specific timing requirements of the application would provide a more precise justification of real-time capability. Additionally, if references are cited in the text claiming that systems exceeding 30 Hz qualify as real-time, these should be explicitly indicated to clarify the basis for such assertions.
7- The clarification of power consumption at both unit-cell (429 mW) and system (252.352 W) levels is appreciated. Inclusion of breakdowns, potential reductions using low-power components, and scalability analysis are all performed properly, I have no further concerns.
8- The authors have provided a thorough and well-structured clarification regarding the number of trainable parameters in both the linear and nonlinear components of their proposed model.
9- The manuscript still does not include a clear mention of the train–test split ratio, both in the main text and in the supplementary materials. In particular, the number of training samples utilized remains unspecified, which leaves uncertainty regarding the total dataset size employed in the study. Explicitly reporting this information is crucial for evaluating the validity, reproducibility, and generalizability of the findings.
10- When displaying the pre-computed dataset in both Fashion-MNIST and MNIST using the t-SNE visualization, it is evident that the outputs for the linear and nonlinear networks differ considerably. I have a minor suggestion regarding these plots. The color maps used for the linear and nonlinear networks is inconsistent. In particular, the linear layer visualization is presented in grayscale, which significantly reduces readability and makes it more challenging to interpret the class structure. Furthermore, in the Supplementary, the linear layer’s t-SNE plots are displayed using colored plots, whereas in the main text they appear in grayscale. This inconsistency in visualization design detracts from the overall clarity of the work, as if there is a difference between the plots that is not immediately obvious. I therefore strongly recommend revising the figures to employ a consistent and easily interpretable color scheme across both the main text and supplementary sections.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Thank you very much for your valuable suggestions. We have carefully addressed your questions point by point. Please refer to the details as below.
Comment 1.1:
1- There are different values for latency which I found confusing:
-) 4.5 ns nonlinearity latency in the original manuscript. As I understand, that does not reflect the nonlinearity latency and was mentioned by mistake. The actual nonlinearity latency was 2.3 us. Is that correct? If so, total latency (with low speed electronics) would have been 3*2.3 + 2.407 = 9.307μs. Please clarify.
-) 2.48 μs system latency and 17.7 ns nonlinearity latency in the revised manuscript. These seem to be based on new measurements on a complete set of new RF components (high-speed). Basically, a new version of the system has been resubmitted but full system classification measurements have not been repeated. Is that correct?
Response:
Thank you for your insightful question. Your understanding is entirely correct. In the original manuscript, the nonlinear metasurface employs low-speed components (RF amplifier RFFM4527, RF detector LMH2110 and operational amplifier TLV9001). This configuration results in a single-layer nonlinear delay of 2.3 μs and a total system delay of approximately 9.307 μs.
In the first revision, we retain the basic architecture of the nonlinear unit (energy detection and gain control) but replace the components with high-speed RF components, including the RF amplifier HMC326, RF detector LTC5536, and operational amplifier THS3201. As a result, the single-layer nonlinear delay is reduced to 17.7 ns, and the total system delay is reduced to 2.48 μs.
Comment 1.2:
Related to the pervious point: On page 13 of the rebuttal, the authors mention: “This functional equivalence ensures our previously demonstrated performance enhancements (in image classification and in action recognition) remain valid, while achieving a faster response speed”. While generally this can be true, to avoid confusion I have the following comment:
As I understand, full system performance measurements have not been repeated with the high-speed version of the system and test boards are fabricated to show faster nonlinearity separately. Is that the case? If so, which is very useful addition to the paper, this should be clarified. The original lower speed components are removed from the revised supplementary document. If full system performance measurements (i.e. classification experiments) have not been redone, the authors should provide the list of both sets of components and their corresponding results. The total system latency and power consumption for both original and new RF components should be provided. This way the reader will fully understand the system capabilities and what has been actually demonstrated.
To summarize, I think it is OK if the authors have not repeated the classification measurement with the high-speed components as long as the they clearly mention that and include all the relevant information for low and high speed results.
Response:
Thank you for your insightful and constructive comments. We sincerely appreciate your kind understanding and supportive suggestion that “It is OK if the authors have not repeated the classification measurement with the high-speed components as long as the they clearly mention that and include all the relevant information for low and high speed results.”
To enhance the completeness of our work and facilitate reader understanding, we took the initiative to conduct full system performance measurements in this revision. All experiments were carried out on the latest version of the high-speed multilayer nonlinear metasurface (as shown in Figs. R1 and R3). Specifically, we repeated all classification tasks (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and posture classification) using the updated high-speed nonlinear network.
The experimental results demonstrate the following:
 Experimental results show that the nonlinear metasurface integrated with high-speed components can fully replace its low-speed counterpart, successfully implementing a ReLU- like activation function with tunable thresholds and slopes.
 Classification experiments further demonstrate that systems integrating high-speed components maintain classification accuracy comparable to low-speed systems in tasks such as image classification and posture recognition, while significantly improving response speed.
 Moreover, under identical input image conditions, the output field distributions of high- speed systems closely match those of low-speed systems, further confirming their functional equivalence in nonlinear operations.
We believe that the additional experiments effectively demonstrate the capability of the nonlinear system employing high-speed devices in classification tasks. The system achieves significantly reduced latency while retaining high classification accuracy. These results also help prevent potential confusion caused by evaluating multiple systems with different delays, ensuring consistent interpretation.
The specific responses include the following four aspects:
(1) Nonlinear metasurface with high-speed components: samples and characterization
(2) MNIST classification using the high-speed system
(3) Fashion-MNIST classification using the high-speed system
(4) Posture recognition using the high-speed system
1. Nonlinear metasurface with high-speed components: samples and characterization
We have fabricated three nonlinear metasurfaces, each integrated with high-speed components, for applications in nonlinear diffractive neural networks. Each metasurface comprises a 14×14 array of units, as illustrated in Figure R1. Specifically, each unit features an LTC5564 RF detector on the front side, while the back side is equipped with an HMC326 RF amplifier and a THS3201 operational amplifier.
Figure R1. Photograph of the nonlinear metasurfaces integrated with high-speed components. a. Front and back views of a single nonlinear unit, showing the high-speed RF detector LTC5564 on the front side, and the high-speed RF amplifier HMC326 together with the high-speed operational amplifier THS3201 on the reverse side. b-d. The transmission coefficient of the nonlinear metasurface was tested within a focused lens antenna system with varying incident intensities, as illustrated in Figure R2a (detailed information of the test system see Supplementary Note 3). By adjusting the incident wave intensity, we measure the transmission coefficient S of the high-speed nonlinear metasurface under different input power 21 levels. A DC power supply is used to provide supply V and control V , enabling the measurement CC BIAS of transmission coefficients under various DC conditions.
As illustrated in Figure R2b, no transmitted energy is detected when the incident power on the metasurface remains below the threshold of 1 mW. Once the input power exceeds this value, the output exhibits a linear increase, effectively mimicking the characteristic behavior of a ReLU activation function in neural networks. This measurement was conducted under a fixed configuration with V set to 0.5 V and V to 5 V. Furthermore, the activation threshold can be dynamically BIAS CC adjusted by the bias voltage, as demonstrated in Figure R2c, where a higher V is shown to reduce BIAS the threshold power. In addition, Figure R2d reveals that increasing V enhances the amplifier gain CC and the transmission coefficient of the metasurface unit. This results in a steeper slope of the nonlinear activation function.
The test results show that the nonlinear metasurface integrated with high-speed components can achieve ReLU-like nonlinear activation, with its threshold and slope being flexibly controlled by the DC voltage. While maintaining reconfigurability comparable to that of low-speed component schemes, this structure also offers the advantage of high-speed response.

2. MNIST classification using the high-speed system
We replace three low-speed nonlinear metasurfaces in the nonlinear network with three high-speed ones for classification experiments. Apart from substituting these three nonlinear metasurfaces, all other settings in the testing system remain unchanged. The constructed high-speed nonlinear network and testing system are shown in Figure R3.

On the MNIST dataset, we test classification accuracy using 5000 random handwritten digits (see Supplementary Note 13 for the rapid detection method). The nonlinear network with high-speed components achieves 92.6% classification accuracy, matching the 92.4% accuracy of the low-speed version and significantly exceeding the linear network’s 88.5% by a margin of 4.1%. These testing results confirm the superior performance of the high-speed nonlinear network. As shown in Figure R4, the output field for digit “4” concentrates strongly in the corresponding region with highest energy, correctly classifying it. Similar results are observed for other images, supporting the effective classification capability of the high-speed nonlinear network.

When processing complex images, the high-speed nonlinear network demonstrates significant advantages compared with linear network. As shown in Figure R5, for a digit “4” sample often mistaken for “9”, the output energy of the high-speed nonlinear network is correctly concentrated in the “4” region. In contrast, the linear network incorrectly produces peak energy in the “9” region, leading to misclassification. Similar behavior is observed in other complex image classification tasks, confirming the superiority of the proposed nonlinear network in handling challenging images. Compared to the nonlinear network based on low-speed components, high-speed one exhibits similar output field distributions. As shown in Figure R6 for the digit “5”, both systems concentrate the maximum field values in the target region, with over 60% of the energy located there. Minor energy differences in other regions (e.g., near the “3”) are negligible and do not impact classification. These slight variations may result from assembly or device inconsistencies. Additional image tests confirm consistent behavior in peak location and energy profile, indicating that the high-speed nonlinear metasurface can effectively replace the low-speed one in implementing the nonlinear activation function.

Question 1: First, if multi-bit recognition is to be performed in future implementations, the proposed system should be analyzed in greater detail, particularly with respect to its processing speed. Response:
Thank you for your insightful suggestions. It should be noted that, if the time during the input and output stages is disregarded, the latency within the diffractive neural network remains the same regardless of whether the input is single-bit or multi-bit. Specifically, it takes 55.53 ns. However, the total end-to-end processing time of the complete system (including input and output) is constrained by the modulation speed of the input layer. Therefore, our response adopts the overall system throughput (encompassing both input and output processes) as the primary performance metric.
Taking the FPGA (Intel Stratix 10) and DAC (Texas Instruments DAC3484) used in the input layer as an example, we provide a detailed analysis of the operation mechanism of the input layer equipped with the DACs, and report the processing speeds (in bps) for each layer of the system: the input layer operates at 7.47 Gbps, the nonlinear layer at 177.2 Gbps, the linear layer at 93.9 Tbps, and the output layer at 41.7 Mbps. Detailed analysis and calculations are presented below.
Detailed operation principle of the DAC-equipped system
The system employs FPGAs to control multiple multi-channel DAC chips, achieving high-precision output across 196 analog voltage channels. By utilizing high-speed FPGAs and high-performance DACs, the system enables rapid voltage configuration, thereby facilitating fast multi-bit amplitude control at the metasurface input layer. The procedure is shown in Figure R12. The grayscale data of the input image is first mapped to the transmission coefficients of the input metasurface with 14×14 unit. Then these coefficients are converted into corresponding analog voltages for each unit based on a predefined relationship between transmission coefficient and amplifier control voltage, as provided in Supplementary Note 30. The continuous voltages are discretized at 16-bit resolution, generating 196 digital voltage signals, which are grouped and distributed across multiple FPGAs (synchronized via SYNC signals). The FPGAs further partition the signals into 49 groups of control signals (each containing 4 discrete digital voltage values) and transmit them via high-speed LVDS interfaces to 49 quad-channel DAC (DAC3484) chips. Collectively, the 49 DACs generate 196 distinct analog voltage signals, with each DAC producing four individual outputs, which are then precisely applied to the corresponding control ports of the 14×14 metasurface unit array to achieve point-to-point control. This allows 16-bit resolution control over the transmission coefficient of each unit of the input metasurface.
The EM wave passes through the input layer with multi-bit amplitude modulation, then propagates through the diffractive neural network composed of three linear layers and three nonlinear layers arranged alternately, and finally reaches the output layer. The output signal is received by ten small antennas, converted into a voltage signal via RF detectors, and then fed into the analog input ports of an Arduino Due R3 MCU for analog-to-digital conversion.
Figure R12. Operating principle of the input layer with integrated DACs. A multi-bit image is input to the FPGAs, which drive 49 DACs in parallel. Each DAC outputs 4 analog voltages, for a total of 196 channels. These signals control the gain of the metasurface’s 196 units, enabling precise multi-bit amplitude modulation.
Processing speed of each layer
The overall processing flow of its multi-bit input primarily involves three stages: input layer encoding (where the gain of metasurface units is controlled via FPGA and DAC), propagation of EM waves through the diffraction neural network (composed of three interleaved linear and nonlinear layers), and output layer detection. For each layer, the processing speed, which is defined as the number of effective bits output per second (in bits per second), is evaluated layer by layer.
(1) Processing speed of the input layer
The input metasurface layer utilizes a 14×14 pixel image as input, with each pixel controlled by a 16- bit high-speed DAC (DAC3484). The total output information amounts to 14×14×16 = 3136 bits. The system latency primarily consists of three components: FPGA processing delay, DAC conversion delay, and metasurface unit response delay. The FPGAs drive 49 DACs in parallel via high-speed LVDS interfaces, with a signal transmission delay of approximately 10 ns. The digital-to-analog conversion delay per channel of the DAC3484 is about 400 ns [R1]. The configuration delay of the metasurface unit mainly arises from the response of the RF amplifiers HMC326, which is approximately 10 ns [R2]. The total system latency is about 420 ns, with the DAC conversion delay being the dominant component. Based on this, the processing speed of the input layer can be calculated as 3136 bits / 420 ns ≈ 7.47 Gbps.
(2) Processing speed of diffractive layers
In a diffractive neural network, both the input and output of its three linear and three nonlinear layers are analog values (i.e., the amplitude and phase of electromagnetic waves), rather than digital bit representations. To standardize the computational metric, the total number of bits processed per layer is defined to be consistent with that of the input layer, namely 3136 bits.
For a nonlinear layer, the total number of bits processed is 3136 bits, and the processing time is 17.7 ns, resulting in a processing speed of 3136 bits / 17.7 ns = 177.2 Gbps.
For a linear layer, which also processes 3136 bits, the processing time is 33.6 ps, leading to a processing speed of 3136 bits / 33.6 ps = 93.9 Tbps.
(3) Processing speed of output layer
The output layer consists of ten small antennas and their corresponding detectors. The voltage signals output by the detectors are acquired through the analog input ports integrated in the Arduino Due R3 MCU, which features a 10-bit ADC resolution. The total number of bits processed is the product of the number of channels and the ADC resolution, i.e., 10 × 10 = 100 bits. The processing time is approximately 2.4 μs (a detailed calculation of the processing time is provided in Supplementary Note 27). Accordingly, the processing speed is calculated as the total number of bits processed divided by the processing time, i.e., 100 bits / 2.4 μs = 41.7 Mbps.
To improve the processing speed of output layer, high-speed ADCs can replace the MCU's internal ADCs, while a high-performance FPGA enables rapid signal processing (see Supplementary Note 27). This approach would reduce the output layer latency to 3–5 ns and increases the processing speed to 20 Gbps.
Figure R13. Schematic of the diffractive neural network integrating DACs, emphasizing the processing-speed hierarchy. a. Network hierarchy, including an input layer with integrated DACs, three alternating linear and nonlinear layers, and an output layer. b. Processing-speed comparison across the layers.
In summary, the processing speeds of each layer are as follows: the input layer operates at 7.47 Gbps, the nonlinear layer at 177.2 Gbps, the linear layer at 93.9 Tbps, and the output layer at 41.7 Mbps, as illustrated in Figure R13. Although the input layer's processing speed is limited by the integrated DAC performance and is slower than the linear and nonlinear layers in the diffractive neural network, it operates at the Gbps level, enabling high-speed computation. Employing higher-speed DACs (e.g., TI DAC39J84, ADI AD9172) can effectively further enhance the processing performance of the input layer.

Comment 2.6:
While the reported total system delay of 2.48 μs (corresponding to a refresh rate of 403 kHz) demonstrates fast operation, it is important to clarify the concept of real-time performance. Real-time processing is not solely determined by achieving or exceeding a particular frequency threshold (e.g., 30 Hz). Instead, it is defined by the system’s ability to respond to inputs within a bounded and application-specific time window. The latency must consistently satisfy the timing constraints dictated by the intended use case. Although the presented latency values indicate that the system operates well within typical real-time bounds, a discussion explicitly linking these delays to the specific timing requirements of the application would provide a more precise justification of real-time capability. Response:
Thank you for your valuable suggestions. You point out that “Real-time processing is not solely determined by achieving or exceeding a particular frequency threshold (e.g., 30 Hz). Instead, it is defined by the system’s ability to respond to inputs within a bounded and application-specific time window.” We fully agree with this perspective. In response, we have supplemented relevant references and provided a clearer comparison between the delay performance of our system and the timing requirements of specific application scenarios, thereby more rigorously demonstrating its real-time processing capabilities.
In posture recognition, real-time requirements vary by application, with no established standard. Existing studies generally agree that such tasks demand processing rates of several tens of fps and millisecond-level delays to achieve basic real-time performance[R1]-[R10]. Our system’s total delay is merely 2.48 μs, which is at least three orders of magnitude lower than typical application requirements, making it well-suited for a wide range of real-time limb movement recognition scenarios.
Specifically, in practical applications such as AR, VR, game interaction, and real time video analysis, limb movement recognition imposes diverse performance requirements. For instance, VR and AR applications typically require end to end delays below 20 ms, corresponding to a 50 Hz refresh rate, to preserve user immersion and prevent motion sickness[R1]. More demanding scenarios like boxing motion analysis often require frame rates of at least 60 fps to accurately capture rapid movements[R2]. By comparison, widely used systems such as Kinect V1 and V2 operate at 30 fps[R3]-[R5], representing a common real time standard in current limb tracking technologies. It is worth noting that certain applications, such as abnormal behavior detection, can still achieve real time performance even at lower frame rates around 8 fps[R6].
In summary, existing studies typically define real time limb movement recognition as operating within a range of 8 to 60 fps, corresponding to delays spanning tens of milliseconds, with specific requirements depending on task and motion characteristics as detailed in Table 1. By comparison, our method achieves a refresh rate of 403 kHz while maintaining a system delay of only a few microseconds. This represents a reduction in delay of at least three orders of magnitude compared to conventional systems, fully satisfying real time processing requirements for this task.
