Comment 1.4:
The images are binarized. What would happen if the image resolution were higher than just one bit? How would the systems operate? This is an important point as a more realistic application requires higher resolution.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful and forward-looking question. To achieve multi-bit amplitude input functionality, our system architecture can be enhanced by integrating an digital-to-analog converter (DAC) module into the control circuitry of the input-layer metasurface. This implementation allows for precise and continuous gain control of individual units in the input-layer metasurface, supporting high-resolution amplitude modulation essential for more realistic applications. We address the issue from two complementary perspectives:
 Input-layer metasurface hardware is compatible with multi-bit control schemes.
 Analysis of prospective methodologies for achieving such multi-bit control in future systems.
1) Input-layer metasurface hardware is compatible with multi-bit control schemes
We employ a gain-programmable metasurface as the input layer, whose structure is illustrated in Fig. R12a. Each unit consists of a front metallic patch, a back metallic patch, and an RF amplifier connecting them. By adjusting the DC bias voltage of the amplifier (0.1V-3V), we achieve continuous gain tuning from -16 dB to 13 dB at the operating frequency, corresponding to a total transmission coefficient tuning range of 29 dB, as shown in Fig.R12b. This multi-bit amplitude modulation characteristic endows the metasurface with continuously tunable transmission coefficients, thereby providing the system with continuous grayscale input encoding capability. Each unit is equipped with an external control interface, enabling continuous and independent gain tuning of individual RF amplifiers, as shown in Fig.R12c.
Figure R12 | Schematic diagram of the input layer with its parametric characteristics. a, The input layer is constructed using an amplitude-programmable metasurface. Each unit integrates a receiving antenna on the front side, a transmitting antenna on the back side, and an RF amplifier linking the two. The amplifier gain is adjustable via the supply voltage VCC. b, Variation of the transmission coefficient at the resonant frequency with respect to the supply voltage. As the voltage increases from 0.1 V to 3 V, the transmission coefficient improves from −16 dB to 13 dB, demonstrating a dynamic tuning range of 29 dB. c, Circuit wiring design of the input-layer metasurface control system, enabling independent voltage regulation for each unit.
2) Analysis of prospective methodologies for achieving such multi-bit control in future systems
To enable continuous and precise amplitude modulation of the input plane, we propose a high- precision control scheme utilizing a DAC module. The system employs an FPGA or MCU as the main controller, coupled with a high-resolution DAC module (such as AD5328) to form a complete voltage regulation system. As depicted in Fig. R13, the implementation involves three key steps: (1) The FPGA or MCU generates digital control signals, transmitted via standard interfaces (e.g., SPI/I2C) to a 16-bit DAC module; (2) The DAC module converts the digital signals into analog voltages; (3) This precisely controlled voltages are applied to the metasurface unit’s control ports. This precision voltage control approach enables high-resolution multi-bit modulation of the transmission coefficient for each unit in input layer.
Figure R13 | Schematic of the high-precision input control system. The system generates digital control signals via an FPGA or MCU, which are then converted into analog voltage signals through a high-precision DAC module. These signals are applied to the metasurface input layer units, enabling multi-bit precise modulation of the transmission coefficient.
Finally, it should be noted that our system supports two distinct input modalities. The first is the encoded input mode, which is the primary focus of this question. In the future, this mode can be enhanced by integrating a DAC module to achieve high-precision multi-bit input. The second is the direct electromagnetic wave processing mode, where the MN-DNN can directly interpret electromagnetic wave signals in space, eliminating the need for complex encoding conversion processes. This mode enables rapid classification and recognition in applications such as posture identification. These two modalities are tailored for different application scenarios and together form a comprehensive input solution for the system.

Comment 1.5:
The linear and nonlinear networks are trained separately. Is this optimal? Could the authors train the whole network together?
Response:
We sincerely apologize for any potential confusion caused by our previous description and would like to provide a more precise clarification regarding our network architecture and training methodology. In our training protocol, all parameters of the nonlinear network (including those from three linear layers and three nonlinear layers) are jointly optimized in an end-to-end manner. We deliberately design and independently train two structurally distinct networks: a nonlinear network and a linear network. The linear network serves as a control benchmark for performance comparison. Crucially, these two systems remain entirely independent throughout the training process, with no parameter sharing or mutual interference between them.
For the nonlinear network, all parameters are trained together, totaling 1458: 484 for each linear layer and two for each nonlinear layer (threshold and slope), as shown in Fig.R14. Specifically, the nonlinear network employs a composite architecture consisting of three linear layers interleaved with three nonlinear layers. All trainable parameters in this network, including the 14×14 unit phase shift parameters in each linear layer and the activation function thresholds and slope parameters in the nonlinear layers, undergo end-to- end joint optimization through a unified error backpropagation algorithm. This ensures that the parameters of both the linear and nonlinear layers update synchronously and co-optimize as an integrated system. In contrast, the linear network contains only three linear layers, with its trainable parameters limited to the 14×14 unit phase shifts in each layer. These parameters are also trained independently using backpropagation.

Digital training algorithm
Figure R16. Digital training flowchart of the nonlinear system. a, Schematic illustration of nonlinear network training, in which all parameters are updated jointly. b, Equivalent structural block diagram of the nonlinear network. The complete details appear as follows: First, the MNIST dataset is down sampled and binarized (details see Supplementary Note 5). Subsequently, the power and phase distribution generated by the horn antenna excitation at the input plane is multiplied by the processed MNIST dataset (Supplementary Note 10), which serves as the input to the MN-DNN. The nonlinear network consists of 1,458 trainable parameters, with 484 parameters per linear layer and 2 parameters (threshold and slope) per nonlinear layer, yielding a total of 484 × 3 + 2 × 3 = 1,458. During training, the input data is first propagated forward through the network to generate predictions. The model’s performance is evaluated using a weighted composite loss function, combining categorical cross-entropy loss (60%) and mean squared error loss (40%) to balance classification and regression objectives. The total loss is then minimized using the Adam optimizer, initialized with a learning rate of 0.01. By leveraging adaptive moment estimation, the optimizer dynamically adjusts parameter updates based on the first and second moments of the gradients. To enhance convergence, an exponential learning rate decay strategy is employed, where the learning rate decays to 96% of its current value every 100,000 training steps. This approach facilitates rapid initial optimization while enabling finer adjustments in later training phases. Throughout the iterative process, classification accuracy is monitored to assess the alignment between predictions and ground truth labels, providing real-time feedback on model performance. A total of 20 training epochs were conducted in Python.

Comment 1.9:
Authors mention (line 118) that the nonlinearity in neural networks is in milliseconds and microseconds range. What kind of neural network are they referring to? If it is optical, then much faster nonlinearities have been demonstrated. Please clarify.
Response:
We gratefully acknowledge the reviewers’ insightful comment. Concerning the discussion of nonlinear responses at millisecond and microsecond timescales in line 118, we clarify that this refers to conventional nonlinear neural network systems based on photoelectric conversion [R21]-[R23] and MCU/ADC-DAC architectures [R24]. We fully agree with the reviewers’ observation that the field of optical nonlinearity has achieved remarkable progress toward faster timescales. Indeed, cutting-edge techniques such as electro-optic self-modulation [R25], semiconductor carrier modulation [R26], and quantum dot thin-film [R27] approaches have demonstrated ultrafast nonlinear responses at picosecond timescales, significantly advancing the temporal performance of diffractive neural networks.
It should be noted that our study focuses on a nonlinear system operating in the microwave regime, which offers distinct practical advantages. Microwave-based deep neural networks can be seamlessly integrated into real-world applications, including wireless communications, remote sensing, radar imaging, and security screening systems. This analog-domain processing paradigm effectively mitigates the limitations of conventional digital baseband processors, such as excessive hardware complexity and high-power consumption.
Moreover, while most state-of-the-art ultrafast nonlinear systems rely on planar optical computing, our proposed spatial diffractive neural network exhibits two key differentiating features: (1) full three-dimensional spatial processing capability, enabling direct manipulation of free-space electromagnetic waves beyond the constraints of planar architectures, and (2) superior spatial scalability, facilitating the implementation of large-scale trainable nodes. These unique characteristics position our microwave-based system as a complementary approach to existing optical solutions, with promising potential for practical deployment.

Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments regarding the origin of performance improvements in nonlinear networks. To address whether these gains stem from increased network depth or intrinsic nonlinear properties, we perform comprehensive analyses and additional controlled experiments.
A key feature of our architecture is that each nonlinear layer employs globally shared parameters, specifically, all 14×14 units within a nonlinear layer utilize identical threshold and slope values. Thus, adding a nonlinear layer introduces only two trainable parameters (threshold and slope), making its contribution to the total parameter count negligible.
To rigorously decouple the effects of depth from nonlinearity, we design a matched six-layer linear control network with identical parameterization. Specifically, we compared 3 networks:
1) A baseline three-layer linear network (22×22 independently tunable units per layer, 1,452 total parameters);
2) A network comprising three linear layers interleaved with three nonlinear layers, with the nonlinear layers contributing only six extra parameters (total parameters: 1,458);
3) A novel six-layer linear network where the additional three layers apply globally consistent linear modulation (two parameters per layer, aptitude and phase, six in total), maintaining both the total parameter count (1,458) and network depth identical to the nonlinear net.

We systematically evaluate the performance of three network architectures using the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets as benchmark tasks. For MNIST classification, as shown in Fig.R19, the baseline three-layer linear network achieves an accuracy of 88.63%. Extending this to a six-layer linear architecture, where each additional layer introduces only two global modulation parameters (totaling six additional parameters), yields a marginal improvement to 88.9%, representing a gain of less than 0.3%. In contrast, introducing three nonlinear layers (with identical parameter) substantially improves accuracy to 92.81%, corresponding to a 4.18% enhancement. These results demonstrate that performance gains arise primarily from nonlinear transformations rather than increased depth or minor parameter adjustments. A similar pattern emerges for Fashion-MNIST (as shown in Fig.R20).
The three-layer linear baseline achieves 77.43% accuracy, while expanding to six linear layers leads to slight degradation (75.08%), reinforcing that simply adding linear depth fails to improve performance. However, incorporating nonlinear layers boosts accuracy to 78.8%, outperforming purely linear architectures despite equivalent parameter counts.
The systematic comparisons reveal that performance improvements depend critically on nonlinear transformations rather than network depth or parameter increments. These findings underscore the effectiveness of our approach in enhancing network expressivity through targeted nonlinearity incorporation.
Regarding to Supplementary Figures S12 and S13, while the phenomenon that adding nonlinear layers can improve recognition accuracy is indeed well-established in literature, the key innovation of our work lies in the in-depth analysis of the unique role played by nonlinear metasurfaces in diffractive neural networks from a hardware implementation perspective. These experimental results not only reconfirm the general effectiveness of nonlinear layers, but more importantly, they provide empirical validation for our proposed nonlinear metasurface-based hardware architecture.

Comment 2.4:
In the dataset-based recognition tasks for both MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, as outlined in Supplementary Note 4, you describe a process in which the original 28×28-pixel grayscale images are first down sampled to 14×14 pixels using interpolation. Following this, a binarization is applied, where pixel values exceeding a threshold of 0.15 are set to 1. While this down sampling and binarization process is a standard approach in some image processing tasks, it is important to note that the binarization step can have a significant impact on dataset difficulty and model performance. By reducing pixel precision, one inevitably loses valuable information, which could directly contribute to a decrease in recognition accuracy. It would be beneficial to discuss the potential effects of this binarization on the presented results, as understanding its impact is crucial for readers evaluating the robustness of this approach.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewers’ valuable comments. We fully agree that the binarization of input images would impact model performance. To systematically evaluate the effects of down sampling and binarization on recognition performance, we conducted comparative experiments on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets. These experiments employed three types of input: original images, down sampled images, and down sampled and binarized images, tested separately in purely linear and nonlinear networks.
The results reveal distinct performance trends. For Fashion-MNIST, the linear network achieves accuracies of 78.00% (original images), 76.98% (down sampled images), and 74.43% (down sampled + binarized images) for the three input types, as shown in Fig. R21. While the nonlinear network attains 83.71%, 82.68%, and 78.80% respectively Fig.R22. Similarly, on MNIST, the linear network achieves 91.28%, 91.07%, and 88.63% (Fig.R23), whereas the nonlinear network reaches 94.78%, 94.68%, and 92.81% (Fig.R24). These findings demonstrate that while down sampling has a relatively minor effect on accuracy, binarization leads to a more substantial performance decline of 2–5%, consistent with the reviewers’ observation that binarization discards valuable image information.
We adopt binarization primarily for two reasons. First, our study focuses on comparing the relative performance of nonlinear versus linear networks under identical input conditions, making input consistency more critical than absolute accuracy. Second, binarization significantly reduces control circuit complexity, a key consideration for our hardware implementation.
We acknowledge the limitations of this down sampling and binarization process and explicitly discuss the performance trade-offs in the revised manuscript. To address these limitations, we propose future enhancements, including the integration of a DAC module to enable approximately continuous grayscale input processing. This modification, compatible with our current input layer architecture, is expected to preserve richer image details and improve recognition accuracy while retaining circuit simplicity. This refinement will better balance performance and implementation complexity. More details and analyses are available in our response to Comment 1.4.

Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewers’ valuable comments. Regarding your concern about the impact of binarization on model performance, we conduct an in-depth comparative study. Through comprehensive simulation and comparative analysis, we confirm that the reduction in classification accuracy on the Fashion-MNIST dataset is predominantly attributable to the dataset transformation (the downsampling and binarization operations) rather than any fundamental constraints of the MN-DNN model.
We would analyze the MN-DNN’s accuracy from two key aspects:
(1) Performance comparison on traditional digital neural networks
(2) Performance comparison on other nonlinear DNNs
Performance comparison on traditional digital neural networks
To systematically evaluate the respective effects of dataset preprocessing and model architecture, we carefully design a fully connected network (FCN) with comparable parameters to MN-DNN, as well as a more representative CNN model as benchmarks. Specifically, the FCN adopts a three-layer structure of 196-7-10, totaling 1,459 parameters, which is highly comparable to MN-DNN’s 1,458 parameters. Additionally, we construct a CNN architecture (approximately 106,000 parameters) comprising convolutional layers, pooling layers, and fully connected layers to investigate the effects of deeper feature extraction. Both models use the same 14×14 binarized input images as MN-DNN.
The experimental results demonstrate that on the binarized MNIST dataset, the FCN, CNN, and MN-DNN achieve accuracies of 85.97% (FCN, Fig. R25), 93.57% (CNN, Fig.R26), and 92.83% (MN-DNN), respectively. On the more challenging Fashion-MNIST dataset, the accuracies are 75.46% (FCN, Fig.R27), 83.22% (CNN, Fig.R28), and 78.8%(MN-DNN), respectively (see Table R11 for the comparative results). MN-DNN performs comparably to or even better than the nonlinear FCN, while being lower but still competitive with the CNN.
Remarkably, MN-DNN achieves classification performance close to that of traditional digital neural networks, which strongly validates the effectiveness of its architecture. We agree that the performance decline primarily stems from information loss due to the binarization process, rather than inherent limitations in MN-DNN’s design.

Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer’s valuable feedback. In response to the comments regarding the trainable parameters in our model, we have conducted a comprehensive review and analysis. Below, we provide a detailed clarification:
Model Architecture and Parameter Efficiency
The linear component of our model comprises three linear layers, each containing 22×22 = 484 trainable phase parameters constrained within the range [0, 2π]. This results in a total of 1,452 trainable parameters for the linear network, as shown in Fig.R29. In contrast, the nonlinear network extends this structure by introducing three nonlinear layers. Each nonlinear layer consists of 14×14 computational units that operate under a shared state, meaning all units within a layer utilize the same nonlinear threshold and slope. Consequently, each nonlinear layer requires training only two key parameters, the threshold and slope of the ReLU activation function. This design enables the nonlinear network to achieve complex transformations while introducing only six additional parameters, yielding a total of 1,458 trainable parameters, as shown in Fig.R30.

Comparative Efficiency with Traditional Neural Networks
Our model demonstrates remarkable parameter efficiency compared to conventional deep learning architectures. For instance, standard fully connected networks for MNIST classification typically require tens to hundreds of thousands of parameters, while even lightweight CNNs such as LeNet-5 demand approximately 60,000 parameters. In contrast, our architecture achieves competitive performance with only ~1,500 parameters—an order of magnitude reduction in model size. This extreme parameter efficiency positions our model within the TinyML (Tiny Machine Learning), domain, yet it retains high recognition accuracy while significantly improving computational efficiency.
Scalability and Flexibility
Notably, our architecture exhibits exceptional scalability. By adjusting the network dimensions (e.g., expanding each linear layer to 56×56 units), the total trainable parameters can be increased by ~9,414, reaching a scale (~10,000 parameters) comparable to conventional fully connected networks. This flexibility allows the model to maintain its lightweight advantages while adapting to more demanding computational tasks without substantial increases in inference time. Such scalability ensures broad applicability across varying complexity requirements while preserving efficiency.

Supplementary Figure S22 | Output plane power detection device. a, Photograph of the MN-DNN system’s output plane detection device. b, Back view of the output plane detection device. c, Photograph of an individual RF power detection circuit board. d, Photograph of an individual detection circuit board connected to the MCU and LED.
For fast output detection, we replace the conventional two-dimensional near-field scanning platform with a rapid output plane detection device, which measures ten regions on the output plane, as shown in Supplementary Figure 22a. The output plane is positioned 10 cm away from the last layer of the hidden layer. A large acrylic plate is supported at the output plane, with 10 designated areas each equipped with a patch antenna and detector to detect the power distribution across the output plane. Additionally, an MCU and an LED (not shown in the figure, located on the side) are mounted on the setup to provide real-time comparison of the energy in the 10 areas and to display the classification results.
Supplementary Figure S22b depicts a back view of the output plane detection apparatus. 10 patch antennas are secured to an acrylic board using plastic screws, positioned at 10 distinct regions designated for output energy detection. The central frequency of these patch antennas matches the operational frequency of the MN-DNN, which is 5.8GHz. Each patch antenna is interfaced with a circuit board designed to perform RF amplification and RF detection, which transforms the RF energy captured by the patch antenna into an equivalent direct current (DC) voltage. The detection circuits are mounted on L-shaped acrylic panels using plastic screws, which are then affixed to the larger acrylic panel via the same fastening technique. The electrical connections for each detection circuit are configured in parallel to maintain a uniform DC voltage bias across all circuits, thus standardizing the performance characteristics of each detection circuit. Supplementary Figure S22c presents a photographic representation of a detection circuit that incorporates a two-stage amplifier and a detector component.
Supplementary Figure S22d provides a photographic illustration of the interface between the detection circuit, the microcontroller unit (MCU) Arduino DUE R3, and the light-emitting diode (LED). The output voltage from the detection circuit is connected to the MCU's analog-to-digital converter (ADC) input for digitization. This digital signal is then subjected to a comparison process across 10 discrete ports. Based on the port exhibiting the highest voltage reading, the MCU generates a corresponding code to regulate the color of the LED. Additionally, the classification result associated with the port exhibiting the highest voltage value is returned to the computer in real-time through serial communication with the MCU Arduino DUE R3. 
Supplementary Figure S23 illustrates the complete equivalent circuit of the high-speed detection system. The device operates as follows: A host computer communicates with an STM32 MCU via a serial interface, which orchestrates the encoding of the input plane. By precisely modulating the voltage applied to each unit cell in the input layer, the input image is spatially encoded onto the transmission coefficients of the metasurface. EM waves then propagate through the encoded input plane, traversing the diffractive neural network before reaching the output plane. At the output plane, RF signals detected by an array of 10 patch antennas undergo amplification via a two-stage RF amplifier. Each amplification stage provides tunable gain (0–10 dB) through voltage-controlled (V ) regulation, yielding a total adjustable gain of 0–20 dB. This wide dynamic range ensures CTRL robust detection of RF signals across varying intensities. The amplified signals are synchronously sampled and digitized through the MCU’s ADC channels. Classification is determined by identifying the channel with the highest output voltage, with results visually indicated via an LED display and simultaneously logged on the host computer for further analysis. Using this optimized detection system, we demonstrate efficient classification of 5,000 test images using both linear and nonlinear diffractive network configurations, with the nonlinear network achieving superior performance (92.4% accuracy) compared to its linear counterpart (88.5%).

Comment 4.3:
The authors should discuss the key factors that set the lower limit of latency, and how it can be further reduced.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for their insightful discussion and constructive feedback on this key technical challenge.
Lower limit of latency
The fundamental lower bound of system latency is governed by two principal factors: the hardware response characteristics of the nonlinear layer and the EM wave propagation delay in air.
(1) Hardware-induced latency arises from the cumulative delays in the RF amplifier, RF detector, and voltage adder in the nonlinear layer. These are intrinsically constrained by semiconductor physics and parasitic effects in circuit packaging, representing a fundamental physical limitation. However, such delays can be partially reduced through advancements in device fabrication and soldering techniques.
(2) Propagation delay is dictated by the time of flight of EM waves between the input and output layers, with its value depending on the distance between the input and output layers. The delay can be mitigated through design optimizations, such as higher operational frequencies or refined interlayer architectures.
The interplay of these two factors determines the theoretical minimum latency achievable in the system.
Strategies for further latency reduction
To address the challenge of further reducing system latency, we propose a comprehensive optimization framework encompassing device-level enhancements, nonlinear unit structural refinements, and system-level architectural improvements.
(1) Device-Level Optimization
The adoption of high-performance components is critical for minimizing latency at the nonlinear unit level. By integrating ultra-fast operational amplifiers with slew rates exceeding 500 V/μs (response time <200 ps) and planar-deposited n-type silicon Schottky barrier diode detectors (response time <220 ps), alongside replacing conventional RF amplifiers with low-latency RF diode switches, we would achieve a single nonlinear unit delay below 426 ps (Table R18). This approaches the theoretical lower bound for response times in current nonlinear layer implementations.

(2) Nonlinear Unit Structural Optimization
Relaxing the reconfigurability constraints of activation functions enables significant simplification of nonlinear layer. By eliminating operational amplifiers and retaining only essential nonlinear components, such as detectors and Schottky diodes (Fig. R38), we could further reduce single-layer latency to ~226 ps. (3) System-Level Optimization
Moreover, in the design of the system architecture, propagation delay can be decreased by reducing the distance between the input and output layers of the nonlinear diffractive neural network. This reduction is attainable through strategies such as elevating the operational frequency and refining the interlayer configuration, including decreasing layer spacing and streamlining the number of layers, which collectively shorten the signal transmission path.
Overall, the proposed multi-scale optimization strategy, including spanning device selection, nonlinear unit structural refinement, and architectural redesign, provides a systematic approach to achieving sub-nanosecond system latency.

[Discussion]
The system latency can be further reduced through multiple optimization approaches (see Supplementary Note 28 for details). By employing high-performance active components in the nonlinear layer, the time delay can be optimized from the nanosecond down to the picosecond range. For example, using operational amplifiers with high slew rates reduces computational delay to below 200 ps, while fast-response diodes (e.g., rapid Schottky barrier diode detectors) as RF detectors shorten the delay to within 220 ps. Further improvements can be achieved by replacing conventional RF amplifiers with high-speed RF Schottky diode switches (~6 ps), enabling superior response speeds. Theoretical calculations indicate that the single-layer delay can be confined to within 426 ps, comparable to the fastest reported nonlinear layers. With a moderate trade-off in reconfigurability, this delay can be further reduced to 226 ps. Additionally, propagation delay can be effectively minimized by optimizing the nonlinear network architecture, for instance, through increased operational frequency and reduced interlayer spacing, thereby compressing the radial distance between input and output planes.
